rationale:
We already have two Lane A long-forms this week (10-20 and 10-21) and no Lane B yet, so today's long-form is Lane B. I picked the pharmacy-legitimacy topic over the CBS retatrutide lab story. The pharmacy video can rest on settled primary sources that won't change: the FDA's BeSafeRx page, its counterfeit-product warnings and its compounding pages, plus the NABP pharmacy-verification lookup. The CBS story is one day old and built on a single outlet's tests. That fails the fact-check bar for a long-form, so it goes in today's 13:00 lead Short instead (gray-market "what's confirmed" Shorts have a median of 102). This doesn't break the 14-day ban on repeating a Short as a long-form: no Short has covered pharmacy checks. The 10-17 compounded-vs-counterfeit Short and the 10-21 recall Short covered different ground.

The 20:00 Short is a spin-off of today's long-form. That video goes live at 14:00, so the Short can name its exact title and pin its link. The 08:00 Short covers the AAO data on semaglutide and macular degeneration. It's an emerging, low-competition eye topic (eye topics do well on Instagram) that corrects a scare with evidence. It's evidence-first and labelled as a conference abstract and observational. I chose it over another muscle Short because muscle already had Shorts on 10-13, 10-16 and 10-21.

The carousel spends no new research effort. It reuses the verified text of the 10-19 Short on semaglutide 7.2 mg vs tirzepatide (88 views), which also keeps today from being all gray-market.

Mix: two rising pieces (S2, and L1 hooked on this week's USA Today piece), one evergreen piece refreshed with a timely hook (C1), and two myth-correcting pieces (S1, S3). Each pillar is used at most twice, and no body system appears more than once.

Skipped:
- Thanksgiving: better published in early November so it ranks before the search peak.
- Recall Short: already covered on 10-20 and 10-21.
- SURMOUNT-5 stomach side effects: covered as a Short on 10-17, so inside the 30-day window.
- Crime-trial story: thin, with stigma risk.
- Price cuts: dated news that's better around Novo's earnings in early November.

pieces.topic: How to check whether a GLP-1 pharmacy is legitimate: the FDA's BeSafeRx red flags, the NABP pharmacy-licence lookup, and how FDA-approved, compounded and counterfeit semaglutide and tirzepatide differ
pieces.angle: Title (60 characters or fewer): 'Semaglutide or Tirzepatide Online: How to Check a Pharmacy'. Thumbnail: 'Real Pharmacy?' next to a labelled, curious pharmacist character. The S3 CTA must use this exact title. Body: 0–15 s, the dated FDA recall notice as the hook, then the answer: 'a legitimate pharmacy needs a prescription, is state-licensed and has a US pharmacist you can reach'. Sections are chapters named as questions people search. (a) The FDA BeSafeRx signs, quoted word for word. (b) How to check a licence with your state board of pharmacy or the NABP. (c) Approved vs compounded vs counterfeit, in 60–90 s: compounded drugs are not FDA-approved and the FDA does not review them for safety, effectiveness or quality before they're sold; counterfeits are fakes. Then the three FDA counterfeit Ozempic alerts with their dates. (d) 'Research use only' means not for people. (e) Report to FDA MedWatch, or the MHRA Yellow Card in the UK. Common GI side effects of the approved medicines, one line. 'Don't stop, switch or change your medicines on your own.' The full prescriber line. End by naming one already-published Lane B long-form.
pieces.working_title: Is My GLP-1 Pharmacy Legit? What the FDA Says to Check
pieces.why: First Lane B long-form this week. It runs on the strongest Short lane (median 102), uses a searched-phrase title of 60 characters or fewer, and rests on stable FDA and NABP primary pages rather than breaking news. | fact-check: A Lane B evergreen topic with real search demand. The structure is safe and nothing in it explains how to buy. Problems to fix: (1) The hook. As far as I can find, the Oct 21, 2026 USA Today story is a nationwide recall of 22 compounded tirzepatide vials from a pharmacy the FDA warned in Dec 2025. We already ran a compounded tirzepatide recall Short (10-20 S1) and a 'compounded vs counterfeit' Short. The 14-day no-repeat rule means the recall can only be a hook of 15 seconds or less, the compounded-vs-counterfeit part must stay a short section, and the core of the video is pharmacy checks. Credit the recall to the FDA or the company notice, not to USA Today alone. (2) The title names no drug. Our data shows drug-less titles fail, and Lane A/B rules want the searched phrase plus the generic name first. (3) Quote the BeSafeRx red flags word for word from the current FDA BeSafeRx page, with its last-reviewed date: requires no valid prescription, no US state-licensed pharmacist available, not licensed by the state board of pharmacy, prices dramatically lower, no physical US address. Don't paraphrase them. (4) Counterfeit Ozempic alerts I confirmed on fda.gov: Dec 2023 (lot NAR0074, serial 430834149057), Apr 2025 (lot PAR0362, serial starting 51746517) and Dec 2025 (counterfeit 1 mg, lot PAR1229, which is also a real lot number; the EXP/LOT text sits to the left instead of above). Cite each from its own FDA page with its date. (5) If the video uses the claim that about 95% of online pharmacies operate illegally, credit it to the NABP with the report year, or cut it. (6) Present NABP and state-board lookups as ways to verify, not as endorsements. Never show a pharmacy's name or URL on screen.

pieces.topic: Semaglutide and age-related macular degeneration: the AAO 2026 case-control abstract (Epic Cosmos records), where a crude higher odds reversed after adjusting for diabetes, high blood pressure and cholesterol
pieces.angle: Title: 'Do Semaglutide-Type Drugs Affect Macular Degeneration? #shorts'. If the class wording reads too vague, use 'GLP-1 Drugs Like Semaglutide and Macular Degeneration'. Name the drug class correctly in the narration: 'GLP-1 medicines, the class that includes semaglutide and tirzepatide'. Answer within 10 s: 'In a huge records study presented at the eye academy's October 2026 meeting, GLP-1 users at first had higher odds of macular degeneration, 1.68 times. When researchers adjusted for diabetes, blood pressure or cholesterol one at a time, the odds dropped below 1. Adjusting for age pushed them higher again. So it's linked, then unlinked, depending on the math: not proof of harm or protection.' Give each figure with its label ('crude', 'adjusted for diabetes', and so on). Explain confounding in one line. On screen: 'case-control · observational · conference abstract, not peer-reviewed (AAO, Oct 2026) · GLP-1 class · not shown to harm or protect'. Optionally add the peer-reviewed Ophthalmology 2026 semaglutide study, but only with figures checked against the paper. Separate line: the EMA lists NAION, a sudden loss of vision in one eye, as a very rare side effect of semaglutide. Action: keep regular eye exams, and get urgent care for any sudden vision change. One GI line: nausea, diarrhoea and constipation are common. 'Don't stop or change your medicines on your own.' Full prescriber line. 170 words or fewer, no emoji.
pieces.working_title: Semaglutide and Macular Degeneration: What New Data Show #shorts
pieces.why: Fresh (Oct 21), low-competition, evidence-first correction of an eye-safety worry. Body-effect topics do well on Instagram, and eye topics reached 47 views on YouTube and 53 on Instagram. | fact-check: Major scope error. The AAO 2026 abstract (Ruan et al., Carle Illinois; AAO meeting Oct 9–12, 2026, New Orleans; Epic Cosmos, more than 300M patients) studied GLP-1 receptor agonists as a class, not semaglutide. The title and the 'semaglutide users' line misattribute it. The angle is also too tidy. Crude ORs: any AMD 1.68, dry 1.89, wet 1.53. Each adjustment was a single-factor Mantel-Haenszel adjustment: diabetes 0.69 (any) / 0.62 (wet), high blood pressure 0.65/0.59, high cholesterol 0.63/0.57. But adjusting for BMI only weakened it to 1.17, and adjusting for age raised it to 1.94. 'The link reversed' leaves out the factors that pushed the other way. The honest takeaway is that the result depends on which factor is adjusted for, so this abstract can't tell us either way. It is an unreviewed conference abstract. A separate peer-reviewed study (Ophthalmology 2026, Johns Hopkins, semaglutide in adults with type 2 diabetes) reported no statistical link to wet AMD. I couldn't open its full text (403), so the scriptwriter must confirm that study's figures before using any of them. The NAION line is fine: per EMA wording, 'very rare' with semaglutide. Keep it separate from AMD.

pieces.topic: Retatrutide sold online: what CBS News' lab tests found (Oct 21, 2026), and what Lilly and the FDA have confirmed
pieces.angle: Answer within 10 s, credited 'CBS News, Oct 21, 2026': 'CBS had three products sold as retatrutide lab-tested. The two bought online were consistent with a basic standard the researcher made, which isn't the same as Lilly's trial drug. The corner-store vial had no peptide at all, just a filler and 13 colonies of bacteria.' Status, credited to Lilly's July 23, 2026 announcement: 'retatrutide is still investigational and not FDA-approved; Lilly plans to submit to the FDA in early 2027, and a plan to file is not approval.' On screen: 'Q1 2027 (planned filing)'. Route: ask a prescriber about approved options or a clinical trial. 'Not personal advice' plus the full prescriber line. 'Follow for more.' No seller names, no product shots, no doses, no sourcing. 170 words or fewer, no emoji.
pieces.working_title: Retatrutide Online: What CBS's Lab Tests Found #shorts
pieces.why: Highest-momentum radar item (92) in our strongest Short lane. Fast-moving news belongs in a Short rather than the long-form, and the lab results add a fact we haven't published. | fact-check: Confirmed: CBS News published on Oct 21, 2026 ('We bought and tested what was sold as an experimental weight loss drug…'). Three samples were tested: two bought online and one Brooklyn bodega vial ($90, labelled 'research use only, not for human consumption'). The analysis was by University of Iowa scientist Jason Galpin. Two fixes. (1) 'Matched only a basic reference standard' is stronger than the source. CBS says both online samples were 'consistent with a basic standard' Galpin created for retatrutide, which 'isn't the same as' Lilly's trial drug. The bodega vial had no peptide, only phenylacetic acid (a filler) and 13 bacteria colonies. The angle leaves out the bacteria, which is the key safety fact. (2) The Q1 2027 filing plan is not in the CBS piece. Credit it to Lilly's July 23, 2026 announcement (plans to submit to the FDA in the first quarter of 2027), from Lilly's own press release. Also check that the 'not approved by MHRA, Health Canada or TGA' claim is current as of Oct 2026, or limit the status line to the FDA. Lilly's statement in CBS mentions 'two deaths associated with black-market retatrutide'. If used, credit it to Lilly via CBS as Lilly's claim, without stating a cause. Don't name Reset Wellness, the gym or the bodega. No vial close-ups. This adds new facts on top of our earlier Bootleg Reta Short, so the variety guard is fine.

pieces.topic: Is your semaglutide pen real? What the FDA has said about counterfeit Ozempic pens and what to check
pieces.angle: Title: 'Is Your Semaglutide Pen Real? What the FDA Flagged #shorts'. Answer within 10 s: 'The FDA has warned three times, most recently in December 2025, about counterfeit Ozempic found in the US supply chain.' Then the Dec 2025 detail exactly as the FDA wrote it: counterfeit 1 mg pens labelled lot PAR1229, which is also a real lot, so check where the EXP/LOT text sits. On the fake it's to the left of the date and lot, not above. One line: earlier FDA alerts named lots NAR0074 (2023) and PAR0362 (2025), with full details at FDA.gov. FDA advice: get it with a prescription from a state-licensed pharmacy, and report suspected fakes to FDA MedWatch. 'Don't stop or change your medicine on your own; ask your pharmacist or prescriber.' Full prescriber line. Last spoken line: 'Full breakdown: [L1's exact published title], on our channel.' L1's video URL goes in the pinned comment and on description line 1. No seller names, no emoji, 170 words or fewer.
pieces.working_title: Is Your Semaglutide Pen Real? What the FDA Flagged #shorts
pieces.why: Spin-off of L1. It names a drug, adds FDA counterfeit-pen facts our 10-17 Short didn't cover, and sends viewers to today's long-form. | fact-check: Facts confirmed on fda.gov. There are three FDA counterfeit Ozempic warnings: Dec 2023 (lot NAR0074, serial 430834149057; needles also counterfeit, so sterility can't be confirmed), Apr 2025 (lot PAR0362, serials starting 51746517) and Dec 2025 (counterfeit 1 mg seized in the legitimate US supply chain, lot PAR1229, which is also a real lot number; on the fake, the 'EXP/LOT' text is to the left of the date and lot instead of above). Fitting all three lot and serial sets into 170 words risks wrong numbers on screen. Lead with the most recent (Dec 2025) alert and mention that earlier alerts exist. Each alert needs its own FDA page URL, not an index page. Sticking to the FDA's own 'check your pen' instructions is fine. Don't present the lot or serial check as proof that a pen is genuine, because the FDA says PAR1229 is also an authentic lot. The CTA title must exactly match L1's final published title, and S3 can only run if L1 actually goes live at 14:00. Otherwise say 'follow for more'.
